title: Seven weeks
hookLine: he stays near the tree; in a storm the serpent Mucalinda coils around him as shelter

cards: After something enormous happens, a birth, a death, a graduation, a diagnosis, the pull is to rush straight to the next thing. Tell everyone. Make plans.
Post about it. The other choice is to stay, and let it settle. The Buddha has just woken up, under the tree, at dawn.
You might expect him to head for the nearest town to share it. He doesn't. The tradition says he stays right there, near the tree, for seven weeks.
And sometime in those weeks, a great storm rolls in.

teach.b: The later telling gives each week its own place. In the first, he sits on the same seat, taking in the freedom. In another, he stands and gazes at the tree without blinking, in gratitude.
In another, he walks slowly up and down. And in one, he sits beneath a tree called the Mucalinda tree. That's when the storm comes.
For seven days the sky is black, the rain doesn't stop, and cold winds blow. From under the ground comes Mucalinda, the serpent king who lives there, a naga, a great snake-being of Indian tradition.

teach.h: MUCALINDA COILS AND SPREADS HIS HOOD.
teach.b: He coils his long body around the Buddha seven times and spreads his great hood over his head like an umbrella. Not to threaten him. To protect him: to keep off the cold, the heat, the flies and the wind.
When the storm passes, the serpent unwinds, takes the form of a young man, and stands before him with joined palms. The scene is told in the Udana, a collection of the Buddha's inspired sayings.
Sculptors in Cambodia and Thailand have carved it in stone and bronze: the Buddha seated on the coils of a great serpent, its many heads fanned out above him like a crown.
The one who has woken up is not alone in the world. After the struggle and the storm, the story lets him be held.

how: Images of the Buddha seated on the coils of the naga Mucalinda are common in Cambodia and Thailand, where the image is also associated with a day of the week, and Buddhists retell the seven weeks as the time he dwelled in the freedom of awakening.

games.q: you're a great serpent living under a tree. a seven-day storm breaks over the awakened one sitting above you. what do you do?
o: coil around him and spread your hood over his head.
wait for the storm to pass, then visit.
games.why: Mucalinda coils around him seven times and spreads his hood like an umbrella. when the storm passes, he takes human form and stands with joined palms.

practice: Find somewhere sheltered to sit if you can, under a roof, near a wall, or wrapped in a blanket, and notice what keeps off the wind and the rain, even the clothes on your skin.
Let yourself feel held by it, the way the Buddha was held by the serpent's coils; you don't have to earn it. Breathe, and let the body soften inside that shelter.

wordCard.voice: Seven weeks. The time the Buddha stayed near the tree after waking, when, in one great storm, the serpent Mucalinda coiled around him as shelter.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the naga king, and of the tree he lived beneath.

carryVoice: Your line: sheltered. A new week starts here: setting the wheel turning.
